title: Olympiad Stars Abdusattorov, Erdogmus Climb On October FIDE Rating List
summary: GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus are the stars on an October FIDE rating list dominated by the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. Abdusattorov climbed two spots to world number-five after picking up 18 rating points and individual gold on board one, while Erdogmus took silver and is now the highest-rated 15-year-old ever after picking up 15 points and moving to world number-17. GM Zhu Jiner was the women's star to gain team and individual gold on board one, picking up nine rating points to regain the women's number-two spot behind GM Hou Yifan. GMs Magnus Carlsen and Hikaru Nakamura continue to lead the rating list after skipping the Olympiad, but most of the world elite was in action. FIDE Classical Ratings Top 100: October 2026

title: Man Charged With Stalking Hannah Sayce, Accused Of Making False Drug Report
summary: A man from Melbourne has been charged over an alleged stalking campaign against Australian chess streamer and content creator WCM Hannah Sayce, which reportedly included making false drug allegations and led to her detention in Qatar. Shumsheer Singh Ghumman, 47, faces 35 charges, including stalking, intimidation, and attempting to pervert the course of justice. The Victorian Supreme Court refused him bail on September 23. He denies the allegations and intends to contest them at trial, the Australian Associated Press reported. In refusing bail, Justice Amanda Fox described the alleged offending as "methodical and planned" and found an unacceptable risk to Sayce's safety and of interference with witnesses. Ghumman remains in custody ahead of an October court appearance. According to the Herald Sun, Qatari officials were falsely told that Sayce was carrying drugs hidden inside her chess pieces. Last week, police told the court that Ghumman emailed officials in Qatar, after which Sayce was held in a jail cell upon arriving in Doha. He allegedly also contacted the Icelandic Chess Federation, and Sayce was detained again, AAP reported. The alleged stalking took place between April 2024 and May 2026. Sayce obtained an intervention order against Ghumman in March 2025, but he allegedly continued gathering information about her family, friends, addresses, and travel plans. He also allegedly threatened to use artificial intelligence to monitor her and intimidated her parents and friends. Sayce, 25, has one of the chess world's most remarkable improvement stories. She rose from a 700 Chess.com rating in 2021 to 2200 in 2023, sharing her progress on her Twitch channel. She currently has a 2367 personal best in blitz on Chess.com, while her bullet peak is 2668, set last month. She also has a 1912 FIDE classical rating after playing in several notable over-the-board tournaments, and earned the woman candidate master title in 2025. Her progress has helped her build an impressive following on social media, where she boasts more than 140,000 followers on Instagram, 58,000 on Twitch, and 25,000 subscribers on YouTube. Last year, Sayce was profiled as Chess.com's Creator of the Month, with the Australian explaining that watching The Queen's Gambit and online chess content inspired her to take the game seriously. A friend suggested she try streaming, and she initially broadcast for six or more hours every day, combining her enthusiasm for creating content with a competitive drive to improve. "I'm really happy that I got to take my viewers along with me on that journey too," she said. Sayce has received support from around the chess world, including from fellow creator WFM Anna Cramling. ❤️❤️❤️❤️ She also received support from two-time U.S. Women's Chess Champion WGM Jennifer Shahade. ❤️❤️❤️❤️🙏 Sayce declined to comment to Chess.com at this time.

title: Witty Alien Shocks Carlsen As 9z Globant Wins 4400-Player Chess Club Showdown
summary: 9z Globant, a team with 962 participants, took first place in the first Chess Club Showdown on Wednesday, September 30. The event featured nine esports teams, ranging in size from 151 to 1142 members. Everyone played a two-hour arena of five-minute blitz games. After the arena, 50 players from each of the top two teams played head-to-head matches in rating order to determine the champion. The tournament represented a unique opportunity for amateur club members to take on some of the most famous stars of the game. Amateurs were able to challenge the likes of GMs Magnus Carlsen, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, and Anish Giri. Today a 1300 rated player decided to enter their first online tournament, the Chess Club Showdown.Their third opponent? Magnus Carlsen. Carlsen, the highest-rated player in the event, did not make it through undefeated. He blundered in a winning position against CM Volen Dyulgerov. Dyulgerov, known by his streaming handle Witty Alien, took advantage and celebrated his upset victory.

title: “Theory and Practice of Chess Education” conference begins in Tsaghkadzor
summary: Alongside the 2026 World Schools Chess Championship – Europe, the International Scientific Conference “Theory and Practice of Chess Education” officially commenced in Tsaghkadzor, Armenia, running from October 1–2, 2026. Serving as a cornerstone event during this pivotal year for chess education, the conference brought together experts to discuss cutting-edge tools and methodologies. The primary objective is to explore innovative approaches and establish strategies for implementing chess across various educational settings globally. The event opened with inspiring welcome speeches from key leaders in the field. Lilit Mkrtchyan, representing the Armenian State Pedagogical University, welcomed attendees alongside Andrey Vodianov, Chief Operating Officer of the International School Chess Federation (ISCF), who emphasized the mission to “build bridges” globally. Smbat Lputyan, Director of the Chess Scientific Research Institute, outlined the core philosophy of the event by framing chess through its multifaceted lenses of sport, science, education, art, and culture. He highlighted the evolution of the game from a competitive sport into a multidisciplinary field, emphasizing its profound impact on youth development and critical thinking. A major highlight of the conference was the signing of an Official Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the ISCF, represented by Andrey Vodianov, and the Armenian State Pedagogical University, represented by Lilit Mkrtchyan. This milestone agreement marks a crucial step in turning visionary ideas into practical applications by bridging international chess education initiatives with prestigious academic institutions. Organizers and participants alike expressed great optimism, hoping that this ceremony marks a strong opening for a long, cooperative, and highly successful new era for chess education worldwide.

title: WSTC Europe Day 3: Competitions, tactical masterclasses and high-altitude adventures in Tsaghkadzor
summary: The third day of the European Continental Stage of the FIDE ISCF World Schools Team Championship 2026 elevated the competitive intensity to new heights in Tsaghkadzor, Armenia. With the tournament crossing into its critical second half, Rounds 5 and 6 delivered a captivating blend of strategic competition on the top boards and heartfelt camaraderie off them. As the top players continued their unstoppable runs, the race for the Grand Final slots became an absolute thriller. The morning air in Tsaghkadzor was crisp, but inside the playing hall where Rounds 5 and 6 of the 2026 FIDE ISCF World Schools Team Championship (European Stage), the atmosphere was white-hot as the tournament leaders finally crossed swords. The penultimate day delivered an extraordinary spectacle of junior chess, showcasing immense fighting spirit, sharp tactical vision, and the brutal reality of time-pressure blunders. With crucial qualification points on the line, the round saw uncompromising chess, with an incredibly low draw rate and an abundance of hard-fought games across all boards.  Highlights of Rounds 5 and 6 Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk (12 Points) holds the top spot after Round 6. Damir Bulgak (Board 1) and Katrina Yakovleva (Board 4) maintain an incredible, perfect 6/6 match record. Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 (10 Points) is firmly in second place. Daniel Beniosev continues his spectacular run on Board 2, sitting on an unbeaten 5.5/6. LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico (9 Points) occupies the third position. Their standout performer is Davit Tatvidze, pulling in a vital win today to push his score to 4.5/6. Leading individual board performers The following players have dominated their respective boards across the first six rounds: Tin Biti (OS Spansko Oranice): An exceptional 5.5/6 showing on Board 1. Ioana-Cristiana Pomirleanu (C.N.”Costache Negruzzi”): Dominating Board 4 with a superb 5.5/6 score. Platon Kiritshenko (Tallinna Tonismae Reaalkool): Putting up an elite 5/6 record on Board 3. Let’s have a look at a couple of fragments illustrating the competitive spirit in the event. A real drama unfolded at one of the top boards, in a thrilling game between Gabriel Gabadadze (2071) and Damir Bulgak (2305). Bulgak seized a huge endgame advantage, only to blunder it away with a natural but erroneous 48… Rd2+??, giving White a precious tempo to advance his king. The correct path was 48…Ra5! (or 48…a3!). As played, the position became equal. However, after 49.Kg3 Rd3+ 50.Kh4 a3 51.g5 Rd2 Gabadadze returned the favor by 52.g6?? (instead of the correct 52.Kg3!) and White was losing again. The opponents traded more errors in subsequent play, but eventually Black’s pawns proved to be faster.   Ignacy Krol – Troi Krasniqi At first glance, Black has to retreat with his queen, but Krasniqi uncorked 14… Qxg5! – an unexpected queen sacrifice that completely changed the dynamics of the game. After 15.hgx5 Rxh1+ 16.Kd2 Bd7, Black emerged slightly better. Unsettled, Krol reacted poorly and ended up in a lost position. Luckily for him, Krasniqi failed to capitalize, and after a series of mutual errors, the opponents split the point. Fast & local: FIDE-rated girls’ blitz The tournament hall in Tsaghkadzor shifted to a lightning-fast pace on Thursday evening as the International School Chess Federation (ISCF) hosted an official FIDE-rated Blitz Tournament for the young female players under 14 years of age. They were inspired by Elina Danielian, Armenian chess grandmaster and six-time Armenian women’s champion, who assisted in the organization of this tournament. With a time control of 3 minutes plus a 2-second increment, the event “Smart Moves: Girls Who Lead” featured an all-local lineup, bringing together talented young girl-players from Armenia for an evening of intense, high-speed tactical battles. Every match carried high stakes, forcing players to rely on quick intuition and sharp calculation. The evening concluded with rapid handshakes and shared analysis, highlighting the deep pool of local chess talent driving the sport forward. Rising champions Following yesterday’s tradition of high-level educational seminars, the tournament hall hosted another installment of the popular masterclass series. Under the banner “Rising Champions,” coaches, players, and their parents gathered for a deeply practical, interactive conversation with grandmaster Samvel Ter-Sahakyan, Coach of the Japanese National Chess Team for the 2026 Chess Olympiad. The session moved quickly past basic theory, diving straight into the concrete realities of elite youth development. Ter-Sahakyan shared invaluable personal insights on navigating the transition from talented school player to international competitor, emphasizing the psychological resilience needed to bounce back during grueling team tournaments. Mind games beyond the board: WSTC Kahoot Quiz The chess world is incredibly vast, built upon centuries of brilliant minds, legendary rivalries, and a deeply precious history. Capitalizing on this rich heritage, the young prodigies in Tsaghkadzor took a break from their standard calculations to test their historical wits in a fast-paced, interactive Kahoot quiz. The event gave players a fantastic opportunity to showcase their deep knowledge of the game’s greatest milestones and for the winner – to get a postcard signed by five-time World Champion Viswanathan Anand. Captains and parents take the stage: The evening blitz Stepping out from the sidelines and into the competitive arena, team captains and players’ parents had their own opportunity to shine today in a special evening blitz tournament. The friendly yet fiercely contested event gave the adults a taste of the high-pressure environment their children face daily on the top boards. Trading their coaching notes for chess clocks, the participants demonstrated impressive tactical vision and deep passion for the game, proving that the love for chess runs deep across every generation present in Tsaghkadzor. What’s Next? With six rounds down and only two remaining, the European Continental Stage is hurtling toward an epic finale. The team standings are incredibly compressed, and mathematically, nearly a dozen schools are still within striking distance of the podium. Yet, as the kids gathered for dinner, sharing jokes, analyzing games on pocket sets, and teaching each other phrases in different languages, it was beautifully clear that the memories forged in Tsaghkadzor are already the ultimate prize. Official website: https://worldschoolteam2026.fide.com/

title: Road to Weissenhaus 2027: Freestyle Friday is back
summary: The World Championship race restarts this Friday, and the door is still wide open. Hamburg / Weissenhaus, October 1, 2026 – The race to the 2027 FIDE Freestyle Chess World Championship is back on. Freestyle Friday, the weekly online tournament on Chess.com, returns this Friday, October 2, streamed live on the Freestyle Chess YouTube channel, Chess.com and DAZN, with a direct ticket to Weissenhaus on the line in both the Open and the Women’s fields. Six seats are still open, three in the Open and three in the Women’s field. Ten Fridays remain, and the standings can change fast. “Formula One has its Grand Prix weekends. Chess now has its Fridays. With Freestyle Friday and our online qualifiers, the road to a World Championship becomes a season-long show. That’s the future of the game,” said Dr. Andreas Walker, CEO of Freestyle Chess. Star power from day one Olympiad champion Nodirbek Yakubboev, Hans Niemann, Denis Lazavik and Ian Nepomniachtchi are expected at the opening event. In the Women’s field, Anna Muzychuk and Alexandra Kosteniuk are among the players expected. More top names will join as the series goes on.  How to watch Every Friday brings a live Freestyle Chess show, hosted by a top name who plays in the event while commentating. The line-up includes Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Hans Niemann, Vidit Gujrathi, Anna Cramling, Dina Belenkaya, Oleksandr Bortnyk, and Sagar Shah and Harshit Raja of ChessBase India. Watch live every Friday at 17:00 Central European Time on channels including the Freestyle Chess YouTube channel, Chess.com, and DAZN. How it works Freestyle Friday runs weekly from October 2 to December 4. The top seven then play a knockout final: quarterfinals on December 11, semifinals and the final on December 18. The winner in each field goes to Weissenhaus. Two more chances Two further online qualification tournaments award the remaining four spots: two in the Open and two in the Women’s field. The first runs from November 29 to December 3, the second from January 3 to 7. The destination The Championships will be held at Weissenhaus Private Nature Luxury Resort on Germany’s Baltic coast. The Women’s Championship runs February 5–7, 2027, and the Open follows February 12–14, 2027. Full regulations are available at https://www.freestyle-chess.com/. About Freestyle Chess Freestyle Chess brings more creativity to top-level chess. The pieces on the back rank are shuffled before each game, so memorized openings don’t help, and players have to think from move one. The FIDE Freestyle Chess World Championship features the world’s best players to crown an official Freestyle world champion.

title: Main Decisions of the FIDE General Assembly 2026
summary: The FIDE General Assembly was held on 26–27 September 2026 in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, during the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad and the FIDE Congress 2026. The Congress brought together representatives of FIDE Member Federations, as well as members of the FIDE Council, Zonal Council and FIDE Commissions. The General Assembly agenda included elections, reports and financial matters, membership issues, administrative matters, changes to the FIDE Handbook, the FIDE Chess Olympiad 2030, and other matters. Elections and Appointments The General Assembly took the following decisions concerning the FIDE leadership and commissions: Mr. Timur Turlov was elected FIDE President. Mr. Viswanathan Anand was elected FIDE Deputy President. The following were elected by the General Assembly as FIDE Vice-Presidents: Ms. Yuhua Xu (CHN) • Mr. Michael Khodarkovsky (USA) • Mr. Pavel Kolobkov (RUS) Mr. Yassin Souleiman Hassan (DJI) The following nominees of the FIDE President were elected: Mr. Luigi Maggi (ITA) – Treasurer Ms. Bouchra Kadiri (MAR) – Vice-President/Secretary of the FIDE Council Mr. Mahir Mammedov (AZE) – Vice-President Ms. Carol S. Williams Pesqueira (ARU) – Vice-President Mr. Mykhailo Podolyak (UKR) – Vice-President The following nominees of the FIDE President as Honorary Vice-Presidents of FIDE were proposed for approval by the FIDE Council: Mr. Rustam Kasimdzhanov (UZB) Mr. Javier Ochoa De Echaguen (ESP) Mr. Fouad Fahmi Darwish (UAE) Mr. Michael Stoettinger (AUT) The General Assembly also: Elected Mr. Francois Strydom (RSA) as a Member of the Constitutional Commission. Supported President’s decision to appoint Mr. Jorge Arias (URU) as Secretary of the Constitutional Commission. Changes to the FIDE Charter and Regulations The General Assembly considered a number of proposals concerning the FIDE Charter and regulations. Appointing the Honorary Vice-Presidents of FIDE The General Assembly approved the proposal of the FIDE President, to appoint up to 5 Honorary Vice-Presidents entitled to participate in the work of the Council with all rights, except for voting rights. The list of proposed nominees is mentioned above. Bilingual Institutional Designation The General Assembly approved an amendment to the FIDE Charter concerning the bilingual institutional designation of FIDE, recognising the historical French name of the organisation alongside its English designation. Under the new Article 5.7, whenever FIDE displays its full institutional name together with the FIDE acronym, seal, flag or emblem, the English and French names will be presented jointly as: International Chess Federation / Fédération Internationale des Échecs. The amendment concerns FIDE’s institutional identity and visual representation only. It does not change the status of English as FIDE’s official and working language and does not introduce a general requirement to translate FIDE documents, regulations, decisions, minutes, contracts, correspondence, news or other communications into French. Chess960 Rating The General Assembly approved the establishment of a FIDE rating system for Fischer Random Chess (Chess960), with the condition that the rating system shall be elaborated and implemented no later than 1 June 2027. This responds to the continued growth of the variant and the need for an official competitive rating framework. The proposal was submitted jointly by the German Chess Federation, Icelandic Chess Federation, Norwegian Chess Federation, Irish Chess Union and Faroe Islands Chess Federation. The initiative noted that Chess960 has been growing internationally, while the absence of an official rating system has limited its integration into the wider competitive chess ecosystem. FIDE Chess Olympiad 2030 The General Assembly noted the readiness of the Qatar Chess Association and the Georgia Chess Federation to host the FIDE Chess Olympiad 2030, together with the FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities 2030 and the FIDE Congress 2030. The Assembly instructed the FIDE Management Board to conduct negotiations with the Qatar Chess Association and, subject to the provision of official organisational and financial guarantees, to inform the FIDE Council and sign the respective contract following formal approval. Should the required official guarantees not be provided and the contract not be signed within a reasonable timeframe, the right to sign the contract will pass to the Georgia Chess Federation, subject to the provision of the corresponding organisational and financial guarantees. Extraordinary General Assembly The General Assembly decided that an Extraordinary General Assembly of FIDE will convene online in late 2026. The FIDE Council was instructed to prepare the FIDE budget for 2027 and the provisional FIDE budget for 2028, and submit them for review at the Extraordinary General Assembly. The full list of decisions and the official documentation will be published at a later date.

title: FIDE October 2026 rating list published
summary: The October 2026 rating list was primarily shaped by the recently concluded 46th Chess Olympiad, with both the top 10 Open and Women’s lists seeing some important shifts. Nodirbek Abdusattorov returned to the top five after a three-month absence following his brilliant performance in Samarkand, which earned him individual gold on Board 1 and 18 rating points. He also matched his career-high rating of 2780. Zhu Jiner collected 9 points at the Chess Olympiad and reclaimed the second position in the Women’s list. Just below the top 10 in the Open and Women’s lists, Yağız Kaan Erdoğmuş and Alice Lee continue their rapid ascent in the rankings. The Turkish youngster gained 15 points at the Olympiad to make his debut in the world’s top 20, while Alice Lee earned 14 points and entered the Women’s top 20 for the first time in her career. Biggest rating gains in top 100 Open and Women Mkrtchyan, Mariam WGM ARM 2421 (+47) Alinasab, Mobina WGM IRI 2364 (+47) Kaliakhmet, Elnaz WIM KAZ 2383 (+36) Mohammadi, Melika WIM IRI 2378 (+36) Cori T., Deysi IM PER 2346 (+30) Lu,Miaoyi IM CHN 2400 (+29) Sivanandan, Bodhana WGM ENG 2382 (+28) Yakubboev, Nodirbek GM UZB 2712 (+27) Savitha Shri B IM IND 2405 (+23) Kiolbasa, Oliwia IM POL 2405 (+19) Mariam Mkrtchyan of Armenia was the biggest rating gainer in the September rating period, earning an impressive 47 points in Samarkand to cross the 2400 mark. Mobina Alinasab added the same number of points to her tally after overperforming at the Festival International de l’Apogée – Nîmes-Caissargues-Pont du Gard. The 2400 club gained two more newcomers in September. Lu Miaoyi and Savitha Shri B both shone in Samarkand, collecting 29 and 23 points, respectively, to clear the 2400 barrier. Bodhana Sivanandan became the youngest Woman Grandmaster in history at the age of 11, thanks to her stellar performance at the 46th Chess Olympiad, which earned her 28 rating points. Nodirbek Yakubboev also delivered on home turf, earning 27 rating points and crossing the 2700 mark for the first time in his career. Elnaz Kaliakhmet, Melika Mohammadi, Deysi Cori, and Oliwia Kiolbasa substantially increased their ratings following their strong showings in Samarkand. Visit: https://ratings.fide.com/ Photos: Michal Walusza and Rafal Oleksiewicz

title: Knight to October 8: Saint Louis to host America's chess elite
summary:
A monthlong celebration

Press release by the Saint Louis Chess Club

The nation's top chess players are set to compete in America's most prestigious competitions: the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship and the 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship . Hosted by the Saint Louis Chess Club (STLCC), each field will feature 12 elite players competing over the board from Oct. 8–23, with Round 1 beginning Oct. 9, for a total prize fund of more than $400,000.

"The U.S. Championship and U.S. Women's Championship represent the pinnacle of American chess, bringing together our nation's very best players to compete at the highest level", said Grandmaster (GM) Yasser Seirawan, chief commentator and spokesperson for STLCC. "As we celebrate nearly a year in our newly renovated home, welcome new inductees to the U.S. Chess Hall of Fame and look forward to an entire October filled with chess and cultural events, 2026 promises to be a truly historic year for Saint Louis and for the game of chess".

About the U.S. Championship

The U.S. Championship is one of the strongest national championships in the world by average rating. First held in 1845, it has crowned legends of the game, including the late World Champion Robert "Bobby" James Fischer, four-time US champion Yasser Seirawan and current World No. 2 Hikaru Nakamura. Since 2009, the Saint Louis Chess Club has proudly hosted every edition of the event, awarding millions in prizes and cementing its role as the premier destination for American chess.

The 2026 field will once again bring together the nation's strongest players, including defending and five-time champion GM Fabiano Caruana, three-time champion GM Wesley So and a slate of rising stars ready to test their skills against America's best.

About the U.S. Women's Championship

The U.S. Women's Championship remains the premier showcase for America's top female players. Since first being hosted in Saint Louis in 2009, the event has elevated women's chess in the U.S. The 2026 edition will feature a competitive field led by the highest-rated American player, defending and four-time champion International Master (IM) Carissa Yip, chess prodigy IM Alice Lee and eight-time champion GM Irina Krush.

How to watch the U.S. and U.S. Women's Championships

Fans can experience the 2026 U.S. Championship and U.S. Women's Championship in person at the Saint Louis Chess Club or follow all the action online. Beginning Oct. 9, the championships will feature 11 rounds of classical chess in a round-robin format, with games streamed live daily at 12:20 p.m. CST.

Live coverage will feature play-by-play commentary and analysis from world-renowned commentators Grandmaster (GM) Yasser Seirawan, GM Maurice Ashley and Woman Grandmaster (WGM) Katerina Nemcova. Fans can watch online via the Saint Louis Chess Club's YouTube and Twitch channels.

Fans in Saint Louis can also experience the nation's top grandmasters competing for the 2026 U.S. Championship and U.S. Women's Championship in person at the Saint Louis Chess Club. Daily tickets are now available for purchase for $25, or $10 for STLCC annual members and include access to the playing hall and spectator lounge.

Saint Louis Chess Conference back and better in 2026

The Saint Louis Chess Club , the U.S. Chess Federation and the Kasparov Chess Foundation will present the second annual Saint Louis Chess Conference, taking place Oct. 22–24, 2026 at the Chase Park Plaza in Saint Louis.

The event will bring together more than 250 educators, researchers, and chess enthusiasts from across the country and around the world in America's Chess Capital. This year's conference will feature keynote speaker legendary World Champion Garry Kasparov.

Attendees will also have the opportunity to experience a variety of marquee events and activities, including:

The Future of Women's Chess : From Pipeline to Podium: A conference-opening discussion examining current research, practical initiatives and emerging insights shaping the future of women in chess.

Mind & Body : The Making of a Chess Athlete: A cross-sport conversation exploring the mental preparation, physical discipline, competitive resilience and sustained performance that define elite athletes. It will feature moderator Maurice Ashley and panelists including NFL Hall of Famer Kellen Winslow, WNBA player Aerial Powers, grandmaster and five-time U.S. Chess Champion Fabiano Caruana, grandmaster and University of Missouri-Columbia head chess coach Cristian Chirila, and professional performance coach Seth Makowsky.

Madwoman's Game : Screening and Panel: A screening and discussion centered on Madwoman's Game, a documentary following young chess player Bianca Mitchell-Avila through her journey in chess, competition and life. It will feature Executive Producer Carla Berkowitz, film subject and Executive Producer Bianca Mitchell-Avila and director Zach Zamboni.

Legends to be inducted into U.S. and World Chess Halls of Fame

October will bring another celebration of chess excellence to Saint Louis, with new members inducted into both the U.S. Chess Hall of Fame and World Chess Hall of Fame . The 2026 U.S. Chess Hall of Fame class will honor Montgomery Major and IM Jeremy Silman , while the World Chess Hall of Fame will welcome GMs Ulf Andersson , Boris Gelfand , Nana Ioseliani , Vasyl Ivanchuk and Alexandra Kosteniuk .

The U.S. Chess Hall of Fame induction ceremony and World Chess Hall of Fame induction of Boris Gelfand will take place Oct. 8 during the opening ceremony of the 2026 U.S. and U.S. Women's Chess Championships, while the remainder of the World Chess Hall of Fame inductees will be honored during the closing of the 2026 Saint Louis Chess Conference on Oct. 24. Together, the seven inductees represent generations of excellence and enduring contributions to chess in the United States and around the world.

Championships bookended by legendary Clutch Chess event

The month concludes with Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown running Oct. 27-29, featuring World No. 2 Hikaru Nakamura, five-time U.S. Champion Fabiano Caruana, 2026 Grand Chess Tour champion Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and 2026 Candidates Tournament winner and World Champion challenger Javokhir Sindarov. The players will face off in an 18-game rapid double round-robin competition for $425,000 in prizes, including daily win bonuses and a Champion's Jackpot.

Fans can watch online via the Saint Louis Chess Club's YouTube and Twitch channels, with commentary from sports broadcaster James Dash Patterson and GMs Yasser Seirawan Maurice Ashley. Spectators will be allowed with purchase of a ticket. Tournament tickets are $50 per day or $150 for all three days; VIP tickets are $100 per day or $275 for all three days. An autograph-session-only ticket is $100. Visit the website for full ticket details and information

Visit saintlouischessclub.org or follow the Saint Louis Chess Club social channels for more information on event details and ticket information.

About the Saint Louis Chess Club

The Saint Louis Chess Club is a non-profit, 501(c)(3) organization that is committed to making chess an important part of our community. In addition to providing a forum for the community to play tournaments and casual games, the club also offers chess improvement classes, beginner lessons and special lectures.

Recognizing the cognitive and behavioral benefits of chess, the Saint Louis Chess Club is committed to supporting those chess programs that already exist in area schools while encouraging the development of new in-school and after-school programs. For more information, visit www.saintlouischessclub.org.

About the World Chess Hall of Fame & Galleries

The World Chess Hall of Fame & Galleries (WCHOF) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization committed to building awareness of the cultural and artistic significance of chess. It opened on September 9, 2011, in the Central West End after moving from previous locations in New York, Washington, D.C. and Miami. Housed in a historic 15,900-square-foot residence-turned-business in Saint Louis' Central West End neighborhood, the WCHOF features World Chess Hall of Fame inductees, United States Chess Hall of Fame inductees selected by the U.S. Chess Trust, artifacts from the permanent collection and exhibitions highlighting the great players, historic games and rich cultural history of chess. The WCHOF partners with the Saint Louis Chess Club to provide innovative programming and outreach to local, national and international audiences. For more information, visit worldchesshof.org and on social: Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and YouTube channels.

title: Afghan Olympiad participants arrested after returning home
summary:
Chess considered a form of gambling

The status of chess in Muslim countries is not entirely clear-cut. In some countries, it is well accepted or even strongly promoted, while in others the guardians of religious orthodoxy view the game with suspicion. In the past, chess has at times even been banned in some Islamic countries as a form of gambling. Other Muslim imams have acknowledged that chess may not constitute gambling, but have nevertheless argued that it distracts believers from honouring Allah and should therefore be prohibited. At present, chess has once again been banned in Afghanistan by the ruling Taliban. Chess clubs have been closed, and anyone seen playing the game can face a fine.

Despite the ban, Afghan players competed under the country's traditional tricolour flag in both the open and, remarkably, the women’s section of the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand.

The Afghan players apparently assumed that they would be able to take part in the Olympiad in the neighbouring country without facing consequences. Those players who still live in Afghanistan were also able to leave the country without interference. Most members of the Afghan delegation, however, live abroad.

Afghanistan's open team scored 10 match points and finished 128 th out of 206 teams. The women's team finished 169 th among 189 teams. The number of organised chess players in Afghanistan is small, however. In FIDE's country rankings, the federation is listed in 132 nd place, with 15 rated players. In the women's rankings, Afghanistan stands 168 th , with three players holding Elo ratings. All three ratings are below 1600, meaning that FIDE treated the Afghan women as unrated for the Olympiad.

Reports are now circulating that three of the Afghan participants - Khaibar Farazi, Habibullah Amini and Habibullah Guldoost, the captain of the women's team - were arrested on re-entering their home country for allegedly violating the ban on gambling. The three men were initially detained at the border and had their passports confiscated. They were then placed under house arrest in Kabul pending a decision by the relevant authorities on what punishment should be imposed for the alleged violation.

A fourth member of the team, Mirzaad Sayed Wahabuddin, was meanwhile able to enter the country without incident through a different border crossing. The remaining eight Olympiad participants, including all of Afghanistan's female players, no longer live in Afghanistan and therefore did not face the same problem.

The border guards reportedly acted on direct instructions from the Afghan Taliban government, which only learned after the players had departed that Afghan citizens had publicly played chess under the Afghan flag in Samarkand. The Taliban were said to be angered by this, and perhaps even more by the fact that Afghan women had taken part in chess tournaments abroad without head coverings.

Khaibar Farazi, the country’s leading player and also a well-known television entertainer, and Habibullah Guldoost, captain of the women’s team, brought the case to public attention through the prominent Spanish chess journalist Leontxo García. The Spanish daily El País , for which García has worked as a chess correspondent for decades, reported on the case.

Afghanistan's FIDE delegate, Adzhmal Mangal, told El País that the information surrounding the case had not yet been confirmed and that it was necessary to wait and see how the situation developed. Zaheer Asefi, the team captain who lives in the Netherlands, expressed greater concern.

It remains unclear what punishment the arrested players might face. Under some interpretations of Sharia law, prohibited gambling can be subject to severe penalties, potentially including amputation of the hands.

The International Chess Federation, FIDE, has pledged its support for the detained Afghan players. Spanish Members of the European Parliament are also seeking to raise the case before the European Parliament.

title: Behind the scenes in Samarkand: The Olympiad comes to a close
summary:
The 2026 Chess Olympiad in Samarkand is over. Here are a few impressions from the final days. We see the start of the matches Uzbekistan–Ukraine and India–Hungary in the final round, including a surprisingly relaxed Richard Rapport, who arrived late at the board.

We also see Arne Kähler beating seven-year-old Uzbek talent Mukhammadyusuf Bakhramov in an intense blitz game, while the Uzbek fans celebrate their team's success.

In the evening, during the closing ceremony, Arne had a brief chat with Austria's Konstantin Peyrer and Frederik Svane from Germany, who had just run back from the hotel to fetch his player badge for access to the playing area.

The closing ceremony, with China receiving gold in the Women's section and Uzbekistan in the Open, marked the end of the 2026 Chess Olympiad, and of the ChessBase team's time in Samarkand.

title: FIDE Ratings - October 2026
summary:
The Chess Olympiad provides a good picture of the current strength of the players taking part, though it is, of course, only a snapshot. Some players are in top form, others are not. And players cannot always aim for the best possible individual result, as the team result comes first. Some games were lost because a player had to push a drawn position for a win and took too many risks. In other cases, a good position was agreed drawn because that secured the desired team result.

Most countries fielded their best players at the Olympiad, and the results in Samarkand brought changes at the top of the FIDE rankings. However, not all top players travelled to Samarkand. Neither Carlsen nor Hikaru Nakamura played, and Nakamura has more or less put his professional career on hold. Alireza Firouzja's relationship with the French federation also seems to be over for the time being.

These three top players — numbers one, two and ten in the world — watched the Olympiad from afar, if they watched it at all. So there was no movement for Carlsen, Nakamura or Firouzja, but plenty for many others.

Uzbekistan's success is reflected in the rankings. Javokhir Sindarov, in fourth place, has closed the gap to Fabiano Caruana to just two points. The current World Championship challenger gained four points, while the 2018 runner-up lost five.

Nodirbek Abdusattorov gained 18 points and is now fifth, just behind Sindarov. Wesley So lost a few points in sixth place, while Praggnanandhaa gained a few in seventh. Vincent Keymer lost only three rating points with his result on top board for bronze medallists Germany, but still dropped two places as Abdusattorov and Praggnanandhaa overtook the German number one.

Wei Yi climbed from 12th to ninth, while Arjun Erigaisi dropped out of the top ten after losing 13 rating points. Erigaisi suffered an unfortunate first-round defeat against the little-known Thai player Laohawirapap Prin and then drew most of his subsequent games. But when it mattered, he beat Peter Leko in the final round.

Alongside Abdusattorov, one of the biggest rating gainers in the top 100 was his teammate Nodirbek Yakubboev (+27), who has now joined the 2700 club. Sixteen-year-old Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, the world's strongest junior, was already there and jumped to 17th place after gaining 15 points in Samarkand.

A number of top players were missing from the Women's Olympiad. This was mainly because China sent only one of its very best players, Zhu Jiner, to Samarkand. The Chinese still won gold with what was effectively their second team, while Zhu Jiner moved up to second place behind Hou Yifan. Five Chinese players continue to occupy the top five places in the world rankings.

Ukraine also competed without its best players. Anna Muzychuk remains eighth without having played a game. The three Russians in the top ten — Aleksandra Goryachkina, Kateryna Lagno and Polina Shuvalova — did not play either, as the Russian federation remains suspended over Russia's war against Ukraine.

Among the very top players, the best results apart from Zhu Jiner came from India's Humpy Koneru (+9), Americans Carissa Yip (+16) and Alice Lee (+14), and especially Armenia's Mariam Mkrtchyan (+47). Eleven-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan (+28) also had an outstanding result.
